title: Isolated splenic hydatid disease
case_text:
A 26-year-old female was referred to our radiology clinic with abdominal pain. The physical examination of the patient revealed splenomegaly. Serology of the patient was consistent with hydatid disease, which helped in the interpretation of the imaging findings. Other laboratory results showed no significant abnormality. We performed abdominal ultrasonography (US), contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography (CT), and noncontrast, contrast-enhanced abdominal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Chest X-rays and cranial MRI were also obtained to rule out pulmonary and intracranial involvement.
In US, we observed a well-defined, multivesicular cystic mass in the location of splenic hilus, measuring 12 x 11 cm. The left kidney was compressed and displaced to the inferolateral position (Figure 1). 
On contrast enhanced CT scans, we detected an unenhancing, hypoattenuating mass located in the anterior portion of the spleen. It had well-defined borders and contained multiple, round, daughter cysts in the periphery of the lesion (Figure 2).
T1-and T2-weighted MRI revealed a multiseptated cystic mass in the spleen which had a well-defined capsule, the mass showing no significant contrast enhancement, except some vague signal increase in the septal parts (Figures 3, 4, and 5). The hypointense rim sign, characteristic of hydatic cyst, was best seen in the T2-weighted sequence (Figure 5). Pulmonary, hepatic, intracranial, and other tissue involvement could not be demonstrated at the time of diagnosis.
With these imaging findings, final diagnosis was made as hydatid disease of the spleen, and the patient underwent total splenectomy. The lesion was proved to be hydatic cyst pathologically. Besides surgery, the patient was also on medical treatment with albendazole. The patient was in good health in control examinations during the two years followup period.

You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Echinococcosis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: isolated splenic hydatid disease
